study_identification_part.si4_title: Microstructural mapping of neural pathways in Alzheimer's disease using macrostructure-informed normative tractometry

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To investigate how white matter microstructure and macrostructure are jointly altered in mild cognitive impairment and dementia using a novel macrostructure-informed normative tractometry (MINT) framework, and to compare MINT-derived metrics with univariate diffusion tensor imaging metrics to examine how fiber geometry may impact the interpretation of microstructure.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Linear regression models fitted for each of 100 segments in 30 bundles with harmonized diffusion metrics (9 features: MAE-Shape, MAE-FA, MAE-MD, MAE-RD, MAE-AxD, DTI-FA, DTI-MD, DTI-RD, DTI-AxD) as dependent variables, and diagnosis (DX), age, and sex as independent variables (formula: metric ~ Age + Sex + DX); CN used as reference group compared to MCI and dementia separately; also dementia vs MCI comparison; FDR correction for multiple comparisons across 3000 tests (30 bundles × 100 segments); separate analyses for each cohort; merged cohort analysis using linear mixed models with cohort as random effect and age, sex, DX as fixed effects; quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plots to rank metrics by sensitivity to dementia; partial Spearman rank-order correlations between bundle-averaged diffusion metrics and clinical assessments (CDRsb, ADAS13, MMSE for ADNI; WLDR, SMIR, SMDR for NIMHANS), controlling for age and sex; FDR correction for correlations
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: MINT identified consistent patterns of white matter microstructural and macrostructural abnormalities in MCI and dementia across two independent cohorts, with diffusivity measures (MD, RD) showing the strongest associations with dementia, and joint modeling of microstructure and macrostructure helping to disentangle disease effects from crossing fiber artifacts, particularly for fractional anisotropy.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: In two independent cohorts (ADNI N=730, NIMHANS N=302), MINT revealed widespread white matter abnormalities in MCI and dementia. Mean diffusivity (MD) and radial diffusivity (RD) showed the strongest associations with dementia, with largest effects in temporal lobe pathways (inferior longitudinal fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus, arcuate fasciculus) and corpus callosum. Both DTI-derived and MINT-derived MD measures showed similar patterns, but MINT-derived fractional anisotropy (FA) measures showed fewer significant regions after accounting for macrostructural variations. A paradoxical 'fan-shaped' pattern was observed in projection pathways, where proximal regions showed higher DTI-FA in dementia (contrary to expected WM degeneration), corresponding to areas with lower macrostructural anomalies (MAE-Shape). This pattern, previously reported in the literature, is likely due to crossing fibers at the corona radiata. MAE diffusivity measures showed stronger correlations with episodic memory (WLDR) in the NIMHANS cohort compared to corresponding DTI measures, particularly in temporal and posterior association pathways. MAE-Shape showed significant associations with clinical dementia severity (CDRsb) comparable to DTI-FA, indicating macrostructural changes are associated with neurodegeneration. Findings were largely consistent across ADNI and NIMHANS cohorts despite demographic differences (ADNI older: 74.13±7.93 vs NIMHANS 67.25±7.86 years, p<10^-34), with stronger statistical significance in the larger ADNI sample. Transfer learning with separate fine-tuning per cohort enabled efficient multi-site analysis while accounting for site-specific variations.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Cross-sectional design (longitudinal data available but not analyzed); fornix and cingulum bundles difficult to reconstruct with automated methods and excluded despite showing early aging changes; some bundles (UF, IFOF) showed inconsistent segmentation quality across protocols affecting harmonization; NIMHANS Siemens protocol showed greater protocol differences than Philips; smaller sample size for NIMHANS may affect model encoding of fiber geometry and statistical power; demographic and cognitive assessment differences across cohorts not fully harmonized; confounders like education and lifestyle not available for NIMHANS; single-shell dMRI with b=1000 limits advanced microstructural modeling; partial volume effects near ventricles may affect MD; generalizability of findings across populations uncertain despite two-cohort validation
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Data from repeated visits and new subjects from ADNI3 and ADNI4 will be included in future longitudinal studies... some key bundles, such as the fornix and the cingulum, are difficult to reconstruct using automated methods due to their unique shape and location, although the fornix is a key structure showing early changes in aging... Out of all bundles, the uncinate fasciculus (UF) and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) bundles show the least alignment after ComBat harmonization. This may be due to inconsistent quality of tractography and segmentation of these bundles across all protocols... The NIMHANS Siemens protocol shows the greatest protocol difference when compared to the Philips protocol from the same cohort or the ADNI protocols... Compared to ADNI, fewer subjects in NIMHANS were used for model fine-tuning and statistical analysis... MINT may more effectively encode patterns of whole-brain fiber geometry when a larger sample of healthy controls is used for fine-tuning... Confounders such as education and lifestyle factors are not currently available for the NIMHANS cohort

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Transfer learning approach enables multi-site analysis without sharing raw data; separate fine-tuning per cohort simulates federated learning scenarios; bundle profiles can be shared across sites after local fine-tuning; Q-Q plots provide intuitive ranking of diffusion metrics by sensitivity to disease; visualization using FURY package enables along-tract mapping of effects; model and code publicly available at https://github.com/wendyfyx/MINT

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a methodological study introducing MINT (Macrostructure-Informed Normative Tractometry), a novel framework combining deep learning (VAE with 1D convolutional layers) with tractometry to jointly model white matter microstructure (DTI metrics) and macrostructure (fiber geometry from tractography). Key innovation is using whole-brain normalization and multi-bundle training to encode fiber proximity and crossing patterns. The VAE has 464,408 parameters with asymmetric encoder-decoder architecture. Pretraining on TractoInferno (198 subjects, 6 studies, >100 million streamlines, 24,000 steps) followed by fine-tuning on target cohorts (5,000 steps each). The paper compares 9 diffusion features: 5 MINT-derived MAE scores (Shape, FA, MD, RD, AxD) and 4 traditional DTI measures (FA, MD, RD, AxD). ComBat harmonization applied at the bundle profile level (post-modeling) rather than at the raw data level. The study demonstrates that joint modeling can help disentangle true microstructural changes from artifacts due to crossing fibers and macrostructural variations. Supplementary materials include detailed along-tract visualizations for all metrics and harmonization evaluation. Code and pretrained models are publicly available. The paper addresses an important limitation of standard tractometry by accounting for whole-brain fiber geometry, though some key tracts (fornix, cingulum) remain difficult to reconstruct. The transfer learning approach is particularly relevant for multi-site studies where data sharing is restricted.
